pos: n. (proper name; father of Nehemiah the governor)
etymology: Hebrew Chakalyah, perhaps wait for the LORD or darkness of the LORD; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Hachaliah is known only as the father of Nehemiah: “The words of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah. And it came to pass in the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace” (Nehemiah 1:1). He is named again when the governor heads the list of those who sealed the covenant: “Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah” (Nehemiah 10:1). That is all Scripture says of him. Yet his son's character implies something of the house: a Jew who rose to be cupbearer to the king of Persia, who wept and fasted and prayed when he heard of Jerusalem's broken walls, and who asked to be sent “unto the city of my fathers' sepulchres, that I may build it” (Nehemiah 2:5). Nehemiah spoke of Jerusalem as the city of his fathers' graves; in a foreign court, a father had kept that memory alive in his son. Hachaliah's name is preserved because his son's book begins with it.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Uzziel the goldsmith who repaired the wall)
etymology: Hebrew Charhayah, perhaps the LORD is angry or dried up of the LORD; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Harhaiah is named as the father of one of the wall-builders: “Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall” (Nehemiah 3:8). The chapter is a roll of who built where, and its striking feature is the variety of hands: priests, rulers, perfumers, merchants, daughters, and goldsmiths. A goldsmith's craft is fine work with soft metal; Uzziel set it aside to haul stones and set beams. The goldsmiths appear again at the end of the circuit, repairing between the corner and the sheep gate (Nehemiah 3:32). The reason Nehemiah gives for the speed of the work applies to them all: “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6). Harhaiah's name stands at the head of one stretch of that wall.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Jedaiah, who repaired the wall over against his house)
etymology: Hebrew Charumaph, flat-nosed or slit-nosed, from charam, to slit, and 'aph, nose.
biblical_def: Harumaph is named as the father of a wall-builder: “And next unto them repaired Jedaiah the son of Harumaph, even over against his house. And next unto him repaired Hattush the son of Hashabniah” (Nehemiah 3:10). The phrase “over against his house” recurs through the chapter, and it describes Nehemiah's wise method: each family built the section nearest its own door. A man defends best what lies before his own house, and the whole circuit was raised by households each doing the part in front of them. The name Harumaph, flat-nosed, may describe a feature, as many Hebrew names did; the law barred a priest with a flat nose from the altar, but Harumaph's son was a layman and his work was the wall. The Jedaiah of this verse is not the priestly house of the same name. He is one of the ordinary householders of Jerusalem whose name Scripture writes in the roll of the rebuilt city.

pos: n. (proper name; father of a wall-builder, and a Levite who led the confession of Nehemiah 9)
etymology: Hebrew Chashabneyah, the LORD has regarded me, from chashab, to think, to regard, and Yah.
biblical_def: Hashabniah is the name of two men in Nehemiah. The first is the father of a builder: “And next unto him repaired Hattush the son of Hashabniah” (Nehemiah 3:10). The second is a Levite who led the great confession after the reading of the law: “Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise” (Nehemiah 9:5). The prayer that follows is the longest in the Old Testament outside the Psalms. It begins with God as Creator, “Thou, even thou, art LORD alone” (Nehemiah 9:6), rehearses His faithfulness from Abraham through the wilderness, the conquest, the judges and the kings, and confesses Israel's rebellion at every turn. Hashabniah's name, the LORD has regarded me, is a fitting name for one who led a people to bless God for regarding them when they had not regarded Him.

etymology: Hebrew Gilalay, perhaps rolled or weighty, from galal, to roll.
biblical_def: Gilalai is one of the Levite musicians who marched in the first great company at the dedication of the wall: “And his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them” (Nehemiah 12:36). For the dedication “they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem, to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps” (Nehemiah 12:27). Two companies went round the top of the wall in opposite directions and met at the house of God, and the day ended in great sacrifices and joy, “so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off” (Nehemiah 12:43). Gilalai played instruments made after David's pattern, behind Ezra the scribe. Worship in the restored city was the worship David had ordered, led by the man who had read the law.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a priestly house in the days of Joiakim)
biblical_def: Helkai is a priest who headed the house of Meraioth in the generation after the return: “Of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai” (Nehemiah 12:15). The list is introduced, “And in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers” (Nehemiah 12:12), and it names the heads of the priestly courses a generation after Zerubbabel. Helkai's name means my portion, and it carries the theology of the priesthood in a word. The priests and Levites received no inheritance of land among the tribes, because “the LORD is their inheritance”; their portion was God Himself and the offerings of His house. A priest named Helkai bore that confession in his name: the psalmist's “The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance” was his whole estate. The New Testament extends it to every believer, a royal priesthood whose portion is not in this world.

etymology: Hebrew Chazayah, the LORD sees, from chazah, to see, and Yah.
biblical_def: Hazaiah is a name in the pedigree of Maaseiah, one of the men of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the wall was built: “And Maaseiah the son of Baruch, the son of Colhozeh, the son of Hazaiah, the son of Adaiah, the son of Joiarib, the son of Zechariah, the son of Shiloni” (Nehemiah 11:5). The setting is the repopulating of the holy city. “The rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city” (Nehemiah 11:1), and “the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem” (Nehemiah 11:2). Jerusalem was a ruin to live in, exposed and poor, and those who moved in did so at cost. The long pedigree establishes Maaseiah as a man of Judah of the house of Shelah, so that Judah's inheritance in the city was proven. Hazaiah, the LORD sees, is one generation in that line.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite of Merari, ancestor of the singer Ethan)
etymology: Hebrew Chaggiyyah, feast of the LORD, from chag, feast, and Yah.
biblical_def: Haggiah is a Levite of the house of Merari: “Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son” (1 Chronicles 6:30). His line is given just before the Chronicler records the singers David appointed: “And these are they whom David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD, after that the ark had rest” (1 Chronicles 6:31). Three heads of singers are traced, Heman of Kohath, Asaph of Gershon, and Ethan of Merari, and Haggiah stands in the Merarite line that produced Ethan. The Levites “ministered before the dwelling place of the tabernacle of the congregation with singing, until Solomon had built the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 6:32). Haggiah's name, feast of the LORD, suits a family that came to serve in song at Israel's feasts. The genealogy exists to show that the singers were Levites by descent, appointed by David, not volunteers who chose the office for themselves.

etymology: Hebrew Chazi'el, God sees or vision of God, from chazah, to see, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Haziel is a Levite of the Gershonites, named when David divided the Levites into courses at the end of his reign: “The sons of Shimei; Shelomith, and Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the chief of the fathers of Laadan” (1 Chronicles 23:9). The context explains the list: “And David divided them into courses among the sons of Levi, namely, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari” (1 Chronicles 23:6). With the ark at rest and the temple about to be built, the Levites would no longer carry the tabernacle, and David reorganised them for service in the house. Haziel was one of the heads of fathers in that new order, set over a portion of the Gershonite Levites. His name, God sees, belongs to a man whose life was spent in the place God chose to put His name, among those who waited on the house of the LORD.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite who dwelt in Jerusalem after the return)
etymology: Hebrew Cheresh, silent or craftsman, from charash, to be silent, or to engrave, to devise.
biblical_def: Heresh is a Levite listed among the first to dwell in Jerusalem after the captivity: “And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph” (1 Chronicles 9:15). The chapter opens with the returned exiles who “dwelt in their possessions in their cities”, and turns to those who lived in Jerusalem itself, priests, Levites, porters and singers. Heresh is named beside Mattaniah of the line of Asaph, so he may have belonged to the singers, of whom the Chronicler says they were “employed in that work day and night” (1 Chronicles 9:33). His name is ambiguous in Hebrew, meaning either silent or craftsman; the same root gives both the deaf and the engraver. If he was a singer, a man called silent spent his days lifting his voice to God; if a craftsman, he served in the house of the God who called Bezaleel. Either way, his name is in the roll of those who came home and dwelt in Jerusalem.

corruption_summary: The silent and the skilled are ranked below the speakers; Scripture counts craftsmen and quiet men among the servants of God's house.
corruption_paragraphs: A church shaped by platform culture values the voice above the hand. Heresh's name means silent or craftsman, and he is counted among the Levites who dwelt in Jerusalem and served in the house of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the variety of service in the body. The Spirit filled Bezaleel with wisdom to work in gold and wood, and the hands are as needful as the tongue.
